topic: A2A Agent Networks: State-Aware Routing with Sprix Sage Router

key_points: Deepest independent analysis of the repo: frames SAGE as the mid-execution case nobody else handles — the task is half done and someone must decide whether moving it is worth discarding finished work.

Publishes hard provenance numbers pulled from the GitHub API: repo public 18 Aug 2026, 3,456 stars / 401 forks on 5 Sep, two releases (v0.1.0, v0.3.0 on 28 Aug), eight contributors, 43 commits, MIT, Python 3.10+, zero runtime dependencies.

Critiques the benchmark honestly: in the trajectory replay the progress-aware vs progress-masked utility error bars overlap almost entirely (0.298 ± 0.021 vs 0.291 ± 0.021), so the real signal is in wasted work (0.104 → 0.059, ~43% less) and switch rate (80.1% → 58.4%) — knowing what is done mostly teaches the router to leave things alone.

Explains the boundary between the three routes shifts with progress, artifact portability, specialist advantage and permission/budget constraints, and notes the project labels its own diagram qualitative rather than fitted.
Gap to exploit: article is analysis-first with no implementation walkthrough and it is a hosted-product blog (Zentor) that pivots to a sales CTA.
competitors.title: Sprix SAGE Router: mid-execution routing for A2A networks (moclaw / Zentor analysis)

key_points: Positions SAGE precisely in the stack: A2A solved agent discovery (a directory problem) but left a runtime void — who actually does the work once the handshake is done.

Documents the utility mathematics in detail: each route scores predicted success, then subtracts cost, critical-path latency, risk, context-transfer loss and coordination overhead, with penalties for uncertainty and a reward for exploration.
Explains complementarity over prestige: a team is scored for marginal requirement coverage, not for stacking individually famous agents; trust is contextual and learned per requirement.

Lists the concrete A2A-to-SAGE mapping (AgentCard.skills -> capability vectors, security requirements -> hard permission filters, provider quotes -> structured bids) and notes the prototype returns a decision but does not transmit tasks.
Frames the gap as a 'directory problem': A2A standardizes discovery via Agent Cards, but the runtime question of who does the work after the handshake is unanswered.
Google unveiled A2A in April 2025 and donated the spec, SDKs and tooling to the Linux Foundation two months later; 100+ companies lined up behind it.
SAGE (State-Aware Graph Exchange) sits conceptually above A2A, ingesting live Agent Cards, requirement DAGs and ExecutionState, then emitting a routing decision.
Reference implementation is deliberately austere: a single Python file with no runtime dependencies.

Production mapping sketched: AgentCard.skills -> normalized capability vectors; security requirements -> hard permission filters; supported modes -> compatibility gates; provider quotes -> structured bids (cost, latency, confidence).
The prototype intentionally stops short of transmitting tasks or authenticating endpoints; an external A2A client must execute the selected route via message/send, streaming or polling.
Core claim: most multi-agent systems either freeze a plan at the outset or loop blindly - SAGE re-evaluates while execution is underway.
competitors.title: A2A Connected the Agents. Now Someone Has to Route Them. (heatdrop editorial)

key_points: Authoritative A2A specification — the protocol SAGE sits above; defines Agent Cards, messages, tasks, artifacts, authentication, transport, multi-turn contextId semantics and the task lifecycle.
Specifies protocol-level pieces a routing layer must respect: Agent Card discovery, capability declarations, streaming events, push notifications, and version negotiation (A2A-Version header).
Does NOT define who should work on a task after execution starts — the gap this guide fills; use it as the baseline vocabulary rather than the answer.
competitors.title: Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol Specification v1.0 (authoritative spec)

key_points: Practical implementation reference: A2A runs on JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTPS with SSE for streaming, Agent Cards served at /.well-known/agent-card.json (renamed from agent.json in v0.3), time-to-hello-world about one day with the official a2a-sdk.
Records the lifecycle operators must honour: submitted -> working -> terminal state, and 'always emit a terminal event or the caller waits forever'.
Sharp framing to reuse: 'A2A carries messages, not meaning' — protocol compliance does not deliver shared context, semantic alignment or governance.
Gap to exploit: strong on protocol plumbing, silent on mid-execution routing, ownership transfer and artifact reuse.
competitors.title: A2A Protocol Implementation Guide (Atlan)

key_points: Landscape comparison of MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP and AP2 — useful for positioning SAGE as an A2A-layer decision policy rather than yet another protocol.
Draws the MCP/A2A split cleanly: MCP connects agents to tools and data; A2A coordinates agent-to-agent collaboration, delegation and shared long-running work.
Gap to exploit: broad protocol survey with no runtime routing depth and no benchmark discussion.
competitors.title: AI Agent Protocols Landscape: MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP, AP2 (Stream)

key_points: STRMAC (arXiv 2511.02200, Nov 2025): a state-aware routing framework that encodes evolving system state plus agent expertise embeddings to select the best single agent at each step.
Reports up to 23.8% improvement over baselines and up to 90.1% reduction in data-collection overhead versus exhaustive search.
Useful academic counterweight: STRMAC needs a trained router encoder, whereas SAGE is a dependency-free, auditable, constrained heuristic — a real trade-off to state explicitly in the article.
competitors.title: STRMAC: State-Aware Routing for Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration (arXiv 2511.02200)
Sprix SAGE makes agent routing a stateful scheduling problem (DEV Community / David Diaz)
key_points: Argues the interesting claim is progress-aware replanning: a router that sees only the original prompt cannot distinguish a task that is still cheap to reassign from one where the incumbent holds decisive context.

Capability is modeled as global trust blended with requirement-conditioned trust, calibrated against outcome evidence - avoiding the error of treating one reputation score as transferable across work types.
Team building uses beam search over team prefixes rather than greedy selection, so adding an agent is rewarded for marginally covering uncovered requirements.

Design judgment praised: multi-agent frameworks treat collaboration as an unconditional upgrade, but each added participant adds messages, dependencies and an attribution problem - a router needs an explicit reason NOT to recruit.
Coordination and context-transfer-loss penalties plus exposed communication topology are what supply that reason.
Synthetic benchmark is externally simulated (hidden capabilities, pair effects, nonlinear quality/cost), which is better test design than scoring the router with its own objective.
Critique: online learning raises the confound of whether feedback reflects agent quality, task difficulty or the router's own prior choices - the prototype cannot settle this.
Verdict: credible as an algorithmic sketch, not a demonstration that a learned router can safely improve an agent marketplace under real incentives, unreliable bids and incomplete outcome labels.

competitors.title: wang2122/sprix-sage-router - Sprix SAGE Router (canonical repository)
key_points: Three routing modes in one auditable objective: SELF (incumbent continues), COLLABORATE (incumbent retains ownership, recruits a complementary team), HANDOFF (a peer takes full ownership).

Core algorithm: combines global + requirement-conditioned trust into calibrated capability q(a,r); reused fraction eta(r) = f(r) when the owner is retained, f(r)*tau(r) when the owner changes, where tau is artifact portability.
Utility U = V*p_hat(y=1|x,m,S,z,E) minus penalties for cost, latency, risk, context-transfer loss (H), coordination overhead (O), plus uncertainty-aware exploration terms.
Requirement DAG is jointly scheduled with assignments; work for one agent is serialized while independent agents run concurrently, then team cost and critical-path latency are rechecked.
Repo stats at retrieval (GitHub REST API, 2026-10-01): 4,261 stars, 186 forks, 181 watchers, 2 open issues, 350 KB, created 2026-08-18, last push 2026-08-28, Python, MIT.
Noise-OR, beam search, linear utility, Beta beliefs and logistic regression are explicitly disclaimed as inventions - replaceable implementation mechanisms, not novelty claims.

Roadmap shows what is missing for production: signed Agent Card ingestion, learned task-text embeddings, real A2A adapters, offline replay on anonymized marketplace traces, adversarial-bid/churn/privacy evaluation, distributed router service with observability and human approval gates.

competitors.title: sprix-sage-router project page (codeKK)
key_points: Restates the framing: agent discovery tells a system which agents exist; it does not answer who should work with whom after execution has already begun.
Describes SAGE as the decision layer between A2A discovery and task execution.
Notes Sprix AI is the A2A initiative of 屿智同行, focused on agent discovery, task matching, multi-agent scheduling and transaction mechanisms.
Used to corroborate that the project is positioned as an algorithmic research output, not a production framework.

competitors.title: Sprix SAGE Router review (FollowAgents directory, FA score 69/100)
key_points: Independent (non-vendor) review: 4.3k stars, MIT, Python 3.10+, 'free, no paid service needed', setup effort low, runs in minutes.
Typical use case: an A2A orchestrator team deciding at a checkpoint whether to preserve the incumbent's context or switch to a specialist.

Explicit 'not a fit if': teams needing production A2A execution/auth/secure transport, teams wanting validated performance on real heterogeneous endpoints, teams needing a complete A2A client with discovery, streaming and cancellation.

Lists implemented surface: SAGERouter with DAG scheduling and beam search, requirement-conditioned trust, online success model, audit traces, exportable learning state, and the sprix_a2a.py ExecutionPlan adapter.
Repeats the caveat that published measurements come from synthetic evaluation, not real endpoint evidence.

stats.fact: Google launched the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol in April 2025; the Linux Foundation launched the A2A project on 23 June 2025 with support from more than 100 technology companies.
A2A Protocol v1.0, described as the first stable production-ready version, shipped on 12 March 2026; on 27 August 2026 A2A was accepted as a Growth Stage project at the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF).
The reference a2aproject/A2A repository had 25,977 stars and 2,638 forks as of 2026-10-01, created 2025-03-25.

Sprix SAGE Router (github.com/wang2122/sprix-sage-router) was created on 18 August 2026, published v0.1.0 the same day and v0.3.0 on 28 August 2026, and stood at 4,261 stars, 186 forks, 181 watchers, 43 commits and 2 open issues on 2026-10-01 — MIT licensed, Python 3.10+, zero runtime dependencies.

In the project's 1,000-checkpoint, five-seed trajectory replay, progress-aware SAGE scored utility 0.298 ± 0.021 with 0.059 wasted work, a 58.4% switch rate and a 23.3% deadline-miss rate; the progress-masked variant scored 0.291 ± 0.021 with 0.104 wasted work, an 80.1% switch rate and a 23.6% deadline-miss rate.

Naive baselines in the same replay: 'always continue' reaches only 0.085 utility with a 34.4% deadline-miss rate, 'always hand off' reaches 0.290 utility but wastes 0.130 of the work (the worst in the table), and a hidden-state dynamic oracle upper bound is 0.375.

In the controlled intervention that changes only in-flight completion from 0.0 to 0.9, progress-aware minus progress-masked utility grows from +0.0000 to +0.0684, and the two policies are identical when completion is zero.

Tracking trust per agent per requirement beats one reputation score per agent: Brier 0.0125 ± 0.0018 and selection regret 0.0094 ± 0.0008 versus 0.0355 ± 0.0008 and 0.0310 ± 0.0359 after 500 observations per seed, with zero routing regret for both in the homogeneous negative control.
On the 2,500 independent-task regression suite, learned SAGE reaches 0.613 quality versus 0.577 for a greedy team, 0.491 for static SAGE and 0.332 for incumbent-only.

The project states its own numbers are regression and falsification evidence only: both evaluators are authored with the project and are 'not evidence of real-world superiority' — a publishable evaluation still needs repeated checkpointed executions on heterogeneous real endpoints.

The prototype deliberately does not transmit tasks, authenticate endpoints or verify signatures; an A2A client remains responsible for message/send, streaming, polling, cancellation and secure artifact handling.
The independent STRMAC state-aware routing framework reports up to 23.8% improvement over baselines and up to 90.1% less data-collection overhead than exhaustive search.

Modality-native routing in A2A networks improves task accuracy by 20 percentage points over text-bottleneck baselines (52% vs 32% on a 50-task benchmark) but costs 1.8x latency, and the gain disappears when the reasoning agent is replaced by keyword matching.

SAGE's default candidate prefilter keeps the incumbent, active executors and the highest-relevance peers up to a candidate_limit of 12, bounding the combinatorial search; permissions, failure state and availability remain hard filters even when budget or deadline are relaxed.
Sprix SAGE Router had 4,261 GitHub stars, 186 forks and 181 watchers on 2026-10-01 (created 2026-08-18, last push 2026-08-28) - roughly 4.3k stars in under 7 weeks.
The repository was at 3,814 stars and 434 forks 20 days after creation (counts retrieved 7 September 2026).

angles: Discovery is a directory problem; routing is a scheduling problem. Agent Cards tell you which agents exist, but nothing in the protocol decides who keeps working, who joins late and who should quit while behind.

The mid-execution checkpoint is the design axis. Most orchestrators freeze a plan up front or loop blindly until something works; SAGE makes progress, partial quality, artifact portability, budget, deadline and failures first-class inputs to a decision that can change mid-flight.

A router needs an explicit reason NOT to recruit. Collaboration is usually sold as a free upgrade, but every added participant brings messages, dependencies, conflicting estimates and an attribution problem - coordination overhead and context-transfer loss are what make SELF a defensible answer.

Rerouting mostly means NOT switching. In the published replay the real gain from knowing what is already done is 43% less wasted work and a lower switch rate, not a large utility jump - checkpoint awareness largely teaches the router to leave things alone.

Requirement-conditioned trust beats one reputation score. Success on coding should not establish reliability for research or planning; the repo publishes a convergence study (Brier 0.0125 vs 0.0355) plus a homogeneous negative control where the advantage vanishes.

Read the benchmark like an engineer. The headline tables are synthetic, authored by the project team, and the progress-aware vs progress-masked error bars overlap (0.298 +/- 0.021 vs 0.291 +/- 0.021); the transferable contribution is the benchmark design - held-out evaluator, progress-masked ablation, controlled intervention - not the absolute numbers.

Disambiguate 'router'. The word now means three unrelated things: which model answers a prompt (RouteLLM-style), which LLM agent takes the next step (STRMAC-style state-aware routing), and which peer owns an in-flight A2A task (SAGE). Only the third is this project's claim.
Complementarity over prestige. Teams are scored for marginal requirement coverage, not for stacking individually strong profiles; adding an agent must earn its coordination cost.
Adoption path is unusually cheap. A dependency-free Python package plus a documented Agent Card mapping means an orchestrator can add checkpoint rerouting as a library, not a platform migration.

The prototype stops at the decision. It emits an auditable ExecutionPlan but does not send messages, authenticate endpoints or verify signatures - a real deployment still needs an A2A client, identity and an artifact evaluator providing inflight_quality.

The feedback loop is the unsolved part. The more the router learns from outcomes, the more its decisions depend on trustworthy identity, evaluation and privacy controls open agent networks have not established; feedback may reflect agent quality, task difficulty or the router's own prior choices.

Governance context: A2A moved to the Agentic AI Foundation in August 2026 alongside MCP, so 'which protocol wins' is the wrong question - the open layer is routing, evaluation and accountability above the protocols.

Practical evaluation frame for any candidate router: how much completed work is preserved, at what added cost and recovery latency, with what deadline-miss rate - the four columns SAGE publishes, and the ones a buying team should demand on real endpoints.

Cross-domain corroboration: independent research (STRMAC, MMA2A) shows routing/state-awareness is a first-order variable - up to 23.8% over baselines in collaborative reasoning, and 20pp accuracy from modality-native A2A routing - which raises the stakes on the synthetic-only evidence in SAGE.

research_notes: Brief assembled 2026-10-01 from live HTTP retrieval (urllib/curl, no browser rendering). Primary evidence is the repository itself plus GitHub REST API counts; the three competitor analyses (heatdrop, dev.to, moclaw) are independent but all published within days of the repo's August 2026 launch, so their star figures are snapshots - always date a number. All benchmark figures are synthetic and project-authored; the repo explicitly disclaims them as evidence of real-world superiority. The write-side differentiators are (1) a reproducible Python walkthrough from Agent Card to ExecutionPlan, (2) an honest benchmark reading that separates design rigor from synthetic numbers, and (3) the production gap list.
